claims.text: Interface pinning within DFT-based simulations can predict the melting temperature of high-melting refractory materials accurately.
Interface pinning within DFT-based simulations can predict entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change upon melting.
Interface pinning has a lower computational cost than full thermodynamic integration.
The initial refractory material is in its equilibrium solid phase.
Interface pinning is an enhanced-sampling free-energy technique that can replace full thermodynamic integration.
Interface pinning directly establishes solid-liquid phase coexistence.
The proposed calculations are conducted with DFT-based molecular dynamics near the melting temperature under equilibrium conditions.
A solid-liquid interface mediates phase coexistence in the interface-pinning simulation.
The solid-liquid interface permits extraction of free-energy differences between the phases.
A bias applied by the interface-pinning method stabilizes a mixed solid-liquid configuration by pinning the interface.
The stabilized mixed-phase configuration enables direct extraction of free-energy contributions from the solid and liquid phases.
These free-energy contributions determine melting temperature, fusion entropy, fusion enthalpy, and volume change without lengthy thermodynamic integration.
Interface-pinning results will agree within acceptable uncertainty with results from full thermodynamic integration.
Interface pinning will significantly reduce computational expense relative to full thermodynamic integration.
The approach works effectively when the solid-liquid interface is well-defined.
Complex phase behavior or significant finite-size interface effects may reduce the accuracy of interface pinning.
Convergence and robustness may be uncertain at ultrahigh temperatures and for materials with complex energy landscapes.
